catalog_quote: Hmong has seven phonemic tones, which vary in realization according to whether they are affected by lexical tone melody alternation processes ... or tone leveling processes realized in fast, non-careful speech. ... In contexts where new information is given or a word is relatively important in its context, a pragmatic prominence tends to be placed on the final syllable of a phonological word (though with the exception of certain enclitic clause-final markers such as =os 'CFM:SOFT' if present; see section 3.3 below). ... Given this bias toward monosyllables, identifying word-level features such as stress is less than straightforward, since if the vast majority of words in a clause are monosyllabic, and every word has lexical stress, there will be no meaningful contrast in lexical stress for most of that clause. ... audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all segments of the deciding quotation, the domain quote and the exceptions quote are verbatim in the held White 2021 text at the printed pages given in the locator (59, 70, 75, 76, 79, 80-81, 88; PDF = printed + 37). (2) Deciding source: a 2021 741-pp PhD grammar (Glottolog's top 'grammar' entry for hmon1264) whose phonology chapters include per-syllable duration/intensity/F0 measurements; it explicitly says there is no meaningful lexical stress contrast and describes an optional, pragmatically conditioned final-syllable (iambic-like) word prominence plus seven lexical tones — exactly what the record codes (kind=tonal, prule final prominence, srule initial intensification, =os exception). No JIPA Illustration or dedicated stress study of Green Mong was found; the instrumental literature (Andruski & Ratliff 2000 JIPA; Andruski 2006) concerns tone/phonation. Mortensen 200
